sections.content: You know *estar* + gerund from A1 Unit 19, and in the last lesson you met *ir* + gerund. *Andar* + gerund also means that someone is doing something, but it adds the idea of going around: the action is spread over several days or places, and it has no clear direction. *Anda buscando trabajo* is "He's going around looking for a job". Speakers often add a note of worry or complaint, especially when they say it about someone else: *¿Por qué andas diciendo eso?* is "Why are you going around saying that?". *Andar* can be in any tense. Its preterite has an irregular stem: *anduve*, *anduvo*, *anduvimos*.
sections.title: Going around doing something
andar + gerund
rows: Mi primo anda buscando casa por todas partes.
My cousin is going around looking for a house everywhere.
¿Por qué andas contando chismes de tus vecinos?
Why are you going around telling gossip about your neighbours?
Los vecinos andaban inquietos, preguntando por la obra.
The neighbours were going around uneasy, asking about the building work.
Anduvimos preguntando por el barrio, pero nadie sabía nada.
We went around the neighbourhood asking, but nobody knew anything.

sections.content: Do not mix up *ir* and *andar* with a gerund. *Van arreglando la calle* means the street is being repaired bit by bit, in order. *Andan arreglando la calle* means the workers are around, doing repairs here and there, with no clear order. *Andar* + gerund is also very common in conversation, so it often sounds informal.
